messages.author: 4747a6a388d4ae7b
messages.subject: schools ranking problem using Stan and JAGS
parts:
Hi

I am trying to get an understanding of the performance of Stan in terms of both runtime and chain mixing. I ran the standard school ranking problem from BUGS examples, http://www.openbugs.net/Examples/Schools.html. I used the model file and data file from

jags: http://www.openbugs.net/Examples/Schools.html
stan: https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/tree/master/bugs_examples/vol2/schools

However, I am surprised to find that jags finishes 1000 warm up and 1000 iterations in 10 seconds, while Stan takes 1200 seconds. Both for one chain.

I am running on windows 8 with a 2.4GHz Intel i5 processor and 8G memory.

I further profile the performance using Intel VTune, and I am surprised (again) to find that Stan executes 30 times the floating point operations as Jags (partially explains why it's slow). Is that because Stan uses a different algorithm (HMC) from Jags? Or is there any other reasons?

I am also getting a lot of warnings from running Stan. Is that the issue?

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
Error in function stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Scale parameter[61]  is 0:0, but must be > 0!
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

Thanks very much!
Chris

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: schools ranking problem using Stan and JAGS
parts:
Hi Chris,

When comparing performance, you really want to look at the number of effective samples per second. The error message is only an indicator of a Metropolis rejection, which, as it says, is fine if it occurs sporadically. As I remember it, the schools example doesn't throw these rejections all the time, but just during initialization / warmup.

You will see this error very often (but not exclusively so) when the support of one of your parameters (declared in the parameter block) extends beyond its prior. E.g. real<lower=-4,upper=1> lambda; (parameter block) combined with lambda ~ lognormal(0,1); (model block) will result in non-existent densities and consequent Metropolis rejections. In this case, the following would be correct: real<lower=0> lambda; lambda ~ lognormal(0,1));.

Best,

Luc

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: schools ranking problem using Stan and JAGS
parts:
Hi Chris,

This is described in the Stan manual on page 5 in the subsection called "Convergence Monitoring and Effective Sample Size." I think the high level picture is described well enough in the manual, BDA3, and across this users list where I don't think I'd be adding anything useful.

Perhaps explaining what you need to do will help:
1. Run Stan and JAGS.
2. Calculate the runtime.
3. Calculate the number of effective samples. For Stan, if you're running in RStan or PyStan, the display of the fit object will contain the number of effective samples. If you're using CmdStan, bin/print will print the number of effective samples. For JAGS, after you get the samples, you can run RStan's monitor() function to calculate the number of effective samples.
4. Compare the quantity (runtime / effective samples) for Stan and JAGS.

There is an additional, necessary step between 1 & 2. You'll have to verify that the models are the same and the inferences are the same. The hard part is making sure the Stan program matches the JAGS program including all parts of the joint posterior. Then you'll have to verify that the inferences are the same for all parameters in the model. The comparison is worthless if one program or both are not actually getting the "right" answer.


Hope that helps.




Daniel

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] schools ranking problem using Stan and JAGS
parts:
1. Yes, measure n_eff/second --- both the Coda output for
JAGS and the Stan output for Stan will give you n_eff in
their output.

2. How are you running Stan? Do you have all the optimization
turned on? Are both systems being given the same starting point?
Do both systems converge (R-hat below 1.05 for all parameters)?

3. The messages are coming from the exp() expression in this:

exp(-.5 * (theta + phi * LRT)

underflowing. If this evaluates to less than -800 or so, the
exp() underflows to 0. So one question to ask is whether both
systems, JAGS and BUGS, are getting appropriately into the tails.
If this is happening just during warmup, I wouldn't worry about it.

Was that min.var and max.var somehow being used in the JAGS
model?

4. This model's probably not well identified. phi looks particularly
bad in the BUGS fit (posterior mean -.0026 and posterior sd 0.0029).
(this is being multipled by a factor of order (-30,30) and then exponentiated).
The posteriors for the coefficients beta don't look very well identified, either.

The whole model is fitting a quadratic function of LRT[p] with hierarchical
parameters. The coefficients don't look very well identiied.
It'd be useful to see if the Stan posterior intervals match those
of JAGS.

I'd suggest tightening up those normal(0,100) priors to something
reasonable for the expected coefficient sizes, which in the posterior are
all less than 1. These are just
holdervers from the super-diffuse dnorm(0,0.0001) priors from the BUGS
models.

5. There are a lot of ways to optimize this very out-of-date
Stan code. The biggest and simplest speedup would be to
replace this:

for (m in 1:M) alpha[m] ~ multi_normal(gamma, Sigma);

with

alpha ~ multi_normal(gamma, Sigma);

But really we want to parameterize this all in terms of Cholesky
factors. We don't have a good way to do this with inverse Wisharts,
yet. We'd recommend using the LKJ priors instead (which is why they're
coded more efficiently). They're easier to parameterize to concentrate
mass around the unit correlation matrix and then independently scale.

The general statement of this

gamma ~ multi_normal(gamma_mu, gamma_Sigma);

isn't necessary when gamma_Sigma is set to a diagonal matrix.
This should be replaced with:

gamma ~ normal(0,10);

The BUGS model let you specify gamma_mu and gamma_Sigma as data,
then passed in a zero vector for gamma_mu and a scaled unit
matrix for gamma_Sigma.

6. There are also alternative parameterizations. Is there a multivariate
version of the Matt trick out there?

7. I think we should be computing min.var and max.var.
We could do that a little less hardcoded, I think.

Anyway, the bottom line here is that the Schools model as coded
isn't a good indication of what Stan can do :-) We should fix
this ourselves so it's a better example.


- Bob






One question I have is whether we should stick to exactly
the same model as in JAGS/BUGS?



Yes, this looks like a case where the model's not identified
properly.

- Bob

Hi, Bob, yes, I think if we have problems such as nonidentified models (or, more generally, models that don’t make sense), we should fix them before putting them in the Stan examples, and then we can also add a note saying that the model has changed. Often these examples that “converge in Bugs or Jags in 10 seconds” or whatever, aren’t really converging so well, they’re just working with those particular starting points. We don’t really want to have any models on the stan page that represent bad practice.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] schools ranking problem using Stan and JAGS
parts:
First a theory question --- the posterior shows lp__ ranging
from -180 to -70 --- is that much range indicative of a problem?

I wrote two new versions of the BUGS vol2/schools example.

I'm appending the models. If anyone has any optimization suggestions
or reparameterization suggestions, let me know and I can try them out.

1. Just a more efficient version of the same model. I
tightened the priors a bit, and used a vectorized form
of multi_normal on the precision scale.

2. Rewritten with LKJ priors using a correlation matrix
plus scale parameterization.

In both instances, rejection warnings arise during the first
few warmup iterations from the scale going to 0 in:

Y ~ normal(Ymu, exp(-0.5 * (theta + phi * LRT)));

It's taking a tree depth of 7 or 8 on average, going out to 11
quite often. So we should probably even deepen the
tree depth here to see if we're getting the right fit.

R-hat is good with four chains. The second model takes about
550 seconds for 1000 warmup iterations and 200 seconds for 1000 sampling
iterations. Effective sample sizes with four chains (4000 saved
draws) range from 75 or so for the hierarchical scale to 4000
for theta and phi. That's a pretty lousy 3 seconds/effective sample
after warmup or so.

The sign of phi isn't identified, with a 95% interval of
(-0.008, 0.003). LRT ranges between [-35,35] or so, and then
it's all inside that exp(-0.5 * ...). theta is around 0.6.

The BUGS report in their manual is for 10K runs and our estimates
match reasonably well --- they only provide posterior
summaries for some of the regression coefficients, not the priors,
which are what have low effective sample sizes with Stan.

The above tests were with RStan 2.4.

- Bob


Optimized a bit
----------------

/**
* Schools: ranking school examination results
* http://www.openbugs.info/Examples/Schools.html
*/
data {
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=0> M;
vector[N] LRT;
int school[N];
int School_denom[N, 3];
int School_gender[N, 2];
int VR[N, 2];
real Y[N];
int Gender[N];
cov_matrix[3] R;
}
parameters {
real beta[8];
real<lower=0> theta;
real phi;
vector[3] alpha[M];
vector[3] gamma;
cov_matrix[3] Omega;
}
model {
real Ymu[N];
for(p in 1:N)
Ymu[p] <- alpha[school[p],1]
+ alpha[school[p],2] * LRT[p]
+ alpha[school[p],3] * VR[p,1]
+ beta[1] * LRT[p] * LRT[p]
+ beta[2] * VR[p,2]
+ beta[3] * Gender[p]
+ beta[4] * School_gender[p,1]
+ beta[5] * School_gender[p,2]
+ beta[6] * School_denom[p,1]
+ beta[7] * School_denom[p,2]
+ beta[8] * School_denom[p,3];

Y ~ normal(Ymu, theta); // exp(-0.5 * (theta + phi * LRT)));

# Priors for fixed effects:
beta ~ normal(0, 5);
theta ~ normal(0, 5);
phi ~ normal(0, 5);

# Priors for random coefficients:
alpha ~ multi_normal_prec(gamma, Omega);

# Hyper-priors:
gamma ~ normal(0,5);
Omega ~ wishart(3, R);
}




Modified with LKJ priors and cholesky factors
=================================================

/**
* Schools: ranking school examination results
* http://www.openbugs.info/Examples/Schools.html
*/
data {
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=0> M;
vector[N] LRT;
int school[N];
int School_denom[N, 3];
int School_gender[N, 2];
int VR[N, 2];
real Y[N];
int Gender[N];
cov_matrix[3] R;
}
parameters {
real beta[8];
real theta;
real phi;
vector[3] alpha[M];
vector[3] gamma;
cholesky_factor_corr[3] L_Sigma;
vector<lower=0>[3] sigma_Sigma;
}
model {
real Ymu[N];
for(p in 1:N)
Ymu[p] <- alpha[school[p],1]
+ alpha[school[p],2] * LRT[p]
+ alpha[school[p],3] * VR[p,1]
+ beta[1] * LRT[p] * LRT[p]
+ beta[2] * VR[p,2]
+ beta[3] * Gender[p]
+ beta[4] * School_gender[p,1]
+ beta[5] * School_gender[p,2]
+ beta[6] * School_denom[p,1]
+ beta[7] * School_denom[p,2]
+ beta[8] * School_denom[p,3];

Y ~ normal(Ymu, exp(-0.5 * (theta + phi * LRT)));

# Priors for fixed effects:
beta ~ normal(0, 2.5);
theta ~ normal(0, 2.5);
phi ~ normal(0, 0.1);

# Priors for random coefficients:
alpha ~ multi_normal_cholesky(gamma, diag_pre_multiply(sigma_Sigma, L_Sigma));

# Hyper-priors:
gamma ~ normal(0, 5);
sigma_Sigma ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
L_Sigma ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(3);
}


- Bob

On Sat, Sep 20, 2014 at 9:04 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

First a theory question --- the posterior shows lp__ ranging
from -180 to -70 --- is that much range indicative of a problem?

I wrote two new versions of the BUGS vol2/schools example.

I'm appending the models.  If anyone has any optimization suggestions
or reparameterization suggestions, let me know and I can try them out.

1.  Just a more efficient version of the same model.  I
tightened the priors a bit, and used a vectorized form
of multi_normal on the precision scale.

2.  Rewritten with LKJ priors using a correlation matrix
plus scale parameterization.

In both instances, rejection warnings arise during the first
few warmup iterations from the scale going to 0 in:

  Y ~ normal(Ymu,  exp(-0.5 * (theta + phi * LRT)));

It's taking a tree depth of 7 or 8 on average, going out to 11
quite often.  So we should probably even deepen the
tree depth here to see if we're getting the right fit.

R-hat is good with four chains.  The second model takes about
550 seconds for 1000 warmup iterations and 200 seconds for 1000 sampling
iterations.  Effective sample sizes with four chains (4000 saved
draws) range from 75 or so for the hierarchical scale to 4000
for theta and phi.  That's a pretty lousy 3 seconds/effective sample
after warmup or so.

The sign of phi isn't identified, with a 95% interval of
(-0.008, 0.003).  LRT ranges between [-35,35] or so, and then
it's all inside that exp(-0.5 * ...).  theta is around 0.6.

The BUGS report in their manual is for 10K runs and our estimates
match reasonably well --- they only provide posterior
summaries for some of the regression coefficients, not the priors,
which are what have low effective sample sizes with Stan.

The above tests were with RStan 2.4.

- Bob


Optimized a bit
----------------

/**
 * Schools: ranking school examination results
 * http://www.openbugs.info/Examples/Schools.html
 */
data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  int<lower=0> M;
  vector[N] LRT;
  int school[N];
  int School_denom[N, 3];
  int School_gender[N, 2];
  int VR[N, 2];
  real Y[N];
  int Gender[N];
  cov_matrix[3] R;
}
parameters {
  real beta[8];
  real<lower=0> theta;
  real phi;
  vector[3] alpha[M];
  vector[3] gamma;
  cov_matrix[3] Omega;
}
model {
  real Ymu[N];
  for(p in 1:N)
    Ymu[p] <- alpha[school[p],1]
      + alpha[school[p],2] * LRT[p]
      + alpha[school[p],3] * VR[p,1]
      + beta[1] * LRT[p] * LRT[p]
      + beta[2] * VR[p,2]
      + beta[3] * Gender[p]
      + beta[4] * School_gender[p,1]
      + beta[5] * School_gender[p,2]
      + beta[6] * School_denom[p,1]
      + beta[7] * School_denom[p,2]
      + beta[8] * School_denom[p,3];

  Y ~ normal(Ymu,  theta); // exp(-0.5 * (theta + phi * LRT)));

  # Priors for fixed effects:
  beta ~ normal(0, 5);
  theta ~ normal(0, 5);
  phi ~ normal(0, 5);

  # Priors for random coefficients:
  alpha ~ multi_normal_prec(gamma, Omega);

  # Hyper-priors:
  gamma ~ normal(0,5);
  Omega ~ wishart(3, R);
}




Modified with LKJ priors and cholesky factors
=================================================

/**
 * Schools: ranking school examination results
 * http://www.openbugs.info/Examples/Schools.html
 */
data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  int<lower=0> M;
  vector[N] LRT;
  int school[N];
  int School_denom[N, 3];
  int School_gender[N, 2];
  int VR[N, 2];
  real Y[N];
  int Gender[N];
  cov_matrix[3] R;
}
parameters {
  real beta[8];
  real theta;
  real phi;
  vector[3] alpha[M];
  vector[3] gamma;
  cholesky_factor_corr[3] L_Sigma;
  vector<lower=0>[3] sigma_Sigma;
}
model {
  real Ymu[N];
  for(p in 1:N)
    Ymu[p] <- alpha[school[p],1]
      + alpha[school[p],2] * LRT[p]
      + alpha[school[p],3] * VR[p,1]
      + beta[1] * LRT[p] * LRT[p]
      + beta[2] * VR[p,2]
      + beta[3] * Gender[p]
      + beta[4] * School_gender[p,1]
      + beta[5] * School_gender[p,2]
      + beta[6] * School_denom[p,1]
      + beta[7] * School_denom[p,2]
      + beta[8] * School_denom[p,3];

  Y ~ normal(Ymu,  exp(-0.5 * (theta + phi * LRT)));

  # Priors for fixed effects:
  beta ~ normal(0, 2.5);
  theta ~ normal(0, 2.5);
  phi ~ normal(0, 0.1);

  # Priors for random coefficients:
  alpha ~ multi_normal_cholesky(gamma, diag_pre_multiply(sigma_Sigma, L_Sigma));

  # Hyper-priors:
  gamma ~ normal(0, 5);
  sigma_Sigma ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
  L_Sigma ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(3);
}


- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] schools ranking problem using Stan and JAGS
parts:
On Sunday, September 21, 2014 12:04:11 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
I'm appending the models.  If anyone has any optimization suggestions
or reparameterization suggestions, let me know and I can try them out.

General rule: Do not use any of the variants of multi_normal when the left-hand side is a parameter.

If there is a law in your country that you have to use the inverse Wishart prior for the covariance matrix of multivariate normal coefficients, integrate the evil covariance matrix out:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse-Wishart_distribution#Conjugate_distribution

and write the prior on the coefficients in terms of the inverse scale matrix and degrees of freedom. HMC has difficulty sampling inverse Wishart covariance matrices, so integrating it out helps numerically. But it is still a bad prior theoretically, and the Schools2.stan attachment, still yields bad performance if you run enough chains (i.e. 4 is too few).

Otherwise, decompose the covariance matrix into standard deviations and a Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix but do not use multi_normal_cholesky. If the multivariate distribution is within the elliptical family and the thing is unknown, always utilize the stochastic representation with i.i.d. standard normal primitives. Schools3.stan can be slower in walltime but is much better at effective sample size.

Ben

parts:
On Monday, September 22, 2014 7:55:55 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
This should become part of the FAQ. Very important piece of information. If possible, then it would be really nice to have this trick done directly behind the scenes if applicable.

May I ask why the "stochastic" representation is so much better when the LHS are parameters? Any theoretical insights here?

I guess we could write an elliptical_transformation() function that would do the math slightly more quickly. But you would still have to reparameterize the model to have the right things in the parameters block, so it can't be fully automated.

With NUTS, you always want the parameters to have a scale near 1 and be uncorrelated with other parameters. If you are using a

beta[j] ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma);

hierarchical prior, then beta[j] depends on mu and even worse on Sigma. In particular, for a nearly singular proposal for Sigma, beta[j] has to be nearly linearly dependent (i.e. one of its elements is nearly fixed, given the other elements).

But if you make beta[j] a transformed parameter with

beta[j] <- mu + L * z[j];

then all the elements of z are (a priori) unit-scaled, mutually independent, and independent of L. It really is the multivariate version of the Matt trick with a Cholesky factor of a covariance matrix serving the role of the standard deviation of a scalar. If L gets nearly-singular, then the last element of z[j] is not well-identified by the data but has a standard normal prior in the model block.

Ben

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] schools ranking problem using Stan and JAGS
parts:
Ah, now I get it. Matt for the multi-variate case ... sweet!

What surprised me was that for the Matt trick to work most effectivley, then the mu above should be included, i.e. I had this in my model:

    matrix[3,J] eta;

    eta <- diag_pre_multiply(sigma_eta, LR_eta * xi);

Now eta's were random effects with mean 0 and I wrote in my model 

      kin  <- exp( (lkappa + lalpha_s)/2. + eta[2,j] );
      kout <- exp( (lkappa - lalpha_s)/2. + eta[3,j] );

and similar for eta[1,j]. This was already not so bad, but then I rewrote everything to 

    vector[3] gamma;
    matrix[J,3] Eta;

    gamma[1] <- 0.;
    gamma[2] <- (lkappa + lalpha_s)/2.;
    gamma[3] <- (lkappa - lalpha_s)/2.;

    Eta <- transpose(rep_matrix(gamma, J) + diag_pre_multiply(sigma_eta, LR_eta * xi));

That is, I included as you did the overall mean. This gave me an even further boost in n_eff, albeit I don't really get why this is beneficial. Any idea?

... and of course, if you guys could provide some functions to make such optimization easier, many users will love you for that!

Anyway, I am very pleased with the performance of Stan now (I was all the time), but now Stan is much superior when it comes to multi-variate stuff at least on the problems I have seen.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: schools ranking problem using Stan and JAGS
parts:
Here's what I wrote to stan-dev on the issue of
adding function support for the Ben trick (aka multivariate
non-centered parameterization).

As Ben points out, the obstacle to full automation is that we
don't have a way to write a function that injects parameters and
transformed parameters.

On the other hand, we could forego the transformed parameters
and just have the user declare the raw parameters, then we
could make the transformed parameters local in the function,
and the function could apply the normal(0,1) prior to the raw
parameters. The downside is that it hides the transformed
parameters, which can be the estimands of interest, as in
the BUGS vol2 schools model.

We could also consider some notion of program transform behind
the scenes. It's tricky figuring out how to apply it.
For instance, we might look for

alpha ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma)

where alpha is a parameter and swap out for non-centered.
Then we can look at where Sigma is a parameter and swap out
for a Cholesky factor (assuming we have the priors that were
used for Sigma).

- Bob

> diag_pre_multiply(sigma_Sigma, L_Sigma * z)
>
> because they are (3 x 1), (3 x 3) and (3 x M) respectively.
> Eigen's clever enough to figure this all out on its own
> using expression templates, but Stan's not that clever.
>
> It would be more efficient with a diag_pre_multiply_lower_tri()
> function. In fact, we pretty much need a whole bunch of
> specializations of matrix ops for:
>
> diagonal matrices (as vectors)
> symmetric matrices
> lower-triangular (upper-triangular) matrices
> symmetric, positive definite matrices
> correlation matrices ?
>
> This is a nice modular project someone could take on a little
> bit at a time that'd make a big difference in multivariate modeling
> speed.
>
> Here's the full Ben trick, isolated for inspection:
>
> parameters {
> matrix[3,M] z;

> vector[3] gamma;
> cholesky_factor_corr[3] L_Sigma;
> vector<lower=0>[3] sigma_Sigma;

> ...
> transformed parameters {
> matrix[M,3] alpha;
> alpha <- transpose(rep_matrix(gamma,M)
> + diag_pre_multiply(sigma_Sigma, L_Sigma) * z);
> }
> model {
> to_vector(z) ~ normal(0,1);
>
>
> which produces the equivalent of
>
>
> parameters {

> vector[3] gamma;
> cholesky_factor_corr[3] L_Sigma;
> vector<lower=0>[3] sigma_Sigma;

> matrix[M,3] alpha;
> ...
> model {
> alpha ~ multi_normal(gamma,
> diag_matrix(sigma_Sigma)
> * L_sigma
> * L_sigma'
> * diag_matrix(sigma_Sigma));
>
>
> (I just wrote the latter version this way for clarity --- quad_form_diag
> and multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose would be more efficient.)
>
> Ideally, to make this standard practice, we'd want a function
> with behavior defined by
>
> vector ben_transform(vector mu,
> vector sigma,
> matrix L,
> matrix z) {
> // validate sizes
> return transpose(rep_matrix(mu,cols(z))
> + diag_pre_multiply(sigma, L) * z);
>
> }
>
> But we could write it in C++ with the derivatives all done
> analytically.
>
> It's tempting, but I think not worthwhile to wrap the whole
> thing up with the priors on L and sigma. For example, we've been
> working with models that place distinct informative priors on elements
> of sigma.
>
> - Bob
